title: Digital Marketing Foundations
tagline: Plan, write, measure and run an honest campaign, with practice in every module
summary: Learn the foundations of digital marketing: customers and the marketing mix, the funnel and channels, copywriting, search, social and email, measuring and testing, and planning a campaign. Every module has a hands-on lab.

modules.title: Marketing fundamentals
modules.summary: What marketing is, how to understand customers and how to explain why your offer is worth choosing.
modules.outcome: You can describe a marketing mix, build a customer persona and write a one-sentence value proposition.
modules.intro: Marketing is not the same as advertising. It is the work of understanding what people need and then making, pricing, describing and delivering something they will want. Advertising is only one tool among many.

topics.title: What marketing really is
topics.html:
Definition

Marketing. Creating, communicating and delivering something of value so that customers choose it and keep choosing it, while the business earns a fair return.

Marketing versus selling versus advertising
TermFocusExample
MarketingUnderstanding and serving customers over timeLearning that students want a quiet place to study
SellingClosing one deal nowA waiter suggesting a second cup
AdvertisingPaid messages to reach peopleA sponsored post about the student offer

A business that only advertises, without understanding its customers, is shouting in the dark. Great marketing begins with listening: who is the customer, what do they want, and what stops them?

Tip

If you cannot say in one sentence who your customer is and what problem you solve for them, more advertising will not fix it.

Check what you just learned

1. Which best describes marketing?
  • Understanding and serving customers over time (correct)
  • Only advertising
  • Only discounts
  • Only social media

Marketing is wider than adverts.
keyPoints: Marketing starts with understanding customers; advertising is one tool.
Selling closes a deal; marketing builds the reason to buy.

topics.title: The marketing mix
topics.html:
The 4 Ps (and what each decides)
PQuestion it answersExample for a cafe
ProductWhat exactly are we offering?Chai, snacks, a quiet study corner
PriceWhat will customers pay, and why?Student discount, simple menu prices
PlaceWhere and how can they get it?Near the college, plus delivery
PromotionHow will they hear about it?Instagram, posters, word of mouth

For services, three more Ps are often added: People (who serves the customer), Process (how smooth the experience is) and Physical evidence (what the place and packaging show). Together they are the 7 Ps.

Common mistakes

  • Spending all effort on promotion while the product disappoints.
  • Setting a price without checking what customers think it is worth.
  • Choosing a location because rent is cheap, not because customers are there.
Worked example

Fix the mix, not just the message

A cafe's advertising works but customers do not return.

  1. Check Product: is the chai good?
  2. Check People and Process: is service slow?
  3. Check Place: is the seating comfortable for studying?
  4. Promotion is not the problem; the experience is.

Answer. The 4 Ps work together; weakness in one cancels the others.

Check what you just learned

1. Which P describes where customers can get the product?
  • Product
  • Place (correct)
  • Price
  • Promotion

Place covers the channel and location.
keyPoints: Product, price, place and promotion work together.
Services also depend on people, process and physical evidence.

topics.title: Customers, personas and value
topics.html:
You cannot serve everyone. Segmentation splits a market into groups with similar needs, such as students, office workers and tourists. A persona is a made-up but realistic person who stands for one segment.

What a good persona includes

  • A name and a few facts: age, situation.
  • Goals: what they want to achieve.
  • Frustrations: what gets in the way.
  • Where they spend time and whom they trust.
  • What would make them choose you.
Definition

Value proposition. A clear statement of the benefit you give a specific customer and why it is better than the alternatives.

Worked example

A value proposition

Cafe near a college.

  1. Weak: We serve good chai.
  2. Better: A quiet, affordable place for students to study, with free wifi and sockets at every table.
  3. It names the customer, the benefit and the difference.

Answer. A strong proposition is specific enough that a competitor could not claim it too.

Tip

Test it: can a stranger repeat it in ten words? If not, it is too long.

Positioning is the place your offer holds in the customer's mind compared with the alternatives. A cafe that is the cheapest, a cafe that is the quietest and a cafe that is the most fashionable each occupy a different position, and each attracts a different customer. Choose one position you can honestly own and let every part of the marketing mix reinforce it.

Check what you just learned

1. What is a persona?
  • A real customer's private data
  • A logo
  • A realistic made-up profile of a typical customer (correct)
  • A discount

It stands for a segment.

Key terms: flip and sort

Marketing mix
Product, price, place and promotion
Segment
A group with similar needs
Persona
A made-up typical customer
Value proposition
Why a customer should choose you
Positioning
The place you hold in customers' minds
keyPoints: Segment the market and describe one persona at a time.
A value proposition names who it serves, the benefit and the difference.

modules.title: Channels and the funnel
modules.summary: Follow the customer journey from awareness to loyalty and choose the right channels for each stage.
modules.outcome: You can describe the marketing funnel, classify channels as owned, earned or paid and choose a sensible mix for a small budget.
modules.intro: Customers do not buy the first time they see you. They notice, think, compare, buy and sometimes return. A funnel is a simple picture of that journey, and each stage needs a different kind of marketing.

topics.title: The funnel
topics.html:
What each stage needs
StageCustomer thinksMarketing that fitsMeasure
AwarenessI did not know this existedVideos, posts, search, postersReach, views
ConsiderationIs it right for me?Reviews, comparisons, demosVisits, time on page
ConversionLet me buyOffers, easy checkoutSales, conversion rate
LoyaltyI will come backRewards, service, emailRepeat rate, referrals
Tip

Find the stage where most people drop out. That is where to spend your effort first.

Check what you just learned

1. Reviews on a product page mostly help which stage?
  • Awareness
  • None
  • Loyalty only
  • Consideration (correct)

People compare options using reviews.
keyPoints: Awareness, consideration, conversion and loyalty need different marketing.
Fix the biggest leak in the funnel first.

topics.title: Owned, earned and paid media
topics.html:
Three kinds of media
TypeMeaningExamplesStrengthWeakness
OwnedChannels you controlWebsite, email list, own social accountCheap, lastingSlow to build an audience
EarnedExposure others give youReviews, press, word of mouth, sharesTrustedYou cannot control it
PaidReach you buySearch ads, social ads, sponsorshipFast and targetedStops when you stop paying

A healthy plan uses all three. Paid media can bring people quickly, owned media (an email list, a good website) keeps them, and earned media follows from doing something worth talking about.

Common mistakes

  • Renting your whole audience from one platform and never collecting emails.
  • Buying ads for a website that is slow or confusing.
  • Ignoring reviews, the cheapest and most trusted marketing of all.

Check what you just learned

1. A customer review on a public site is:
  • Earned media (correct)
  • Owned media
  • Paid media
  • Not media

Others created it.

2. Which stops working when you stop paying?
  • Owned
  • Paid (correct)
  • Earned
  • All

Paid reach is rented.
keyPoints: Owned you control; earned others give; paid you buy.
Use all three: paid is fast, owned lasts, earned is trusted.

topics.title: Choosing channels for a small budget
topics.html:
How to choose

  1. Start with your persona: where do they already spend time?
  2. Pick one or two channels, do them well, then add more.
  3. Match the channel to the stage of the funnel you need to fix.
  4. Test with a small budget before you scale.
  5. Keep what is measurable and drop what is not working.
Channel strengths
ChannelBest forCost to start
Search adsPeople already looking for youMedium, pay per click
Social adsReaching new people by interestLow to medium
EmailSelling again to existing customersVery low
Content and SEOLong-term trust and free trafficTime more than money
Local posters and eventsNearby customersLow
Worked example

A cafe with 40,000 for two weeks

Persona: first-year students who live on Instagram and WhatsApp.

  1. Instagram stories and reels, because that is where the persona is.
  2. Posters in the library, for people nearby.
  3. An email to existing student customers, which is almost free.
  4. Search ads skipped: few students search for cafes by name.

Answer. A short list of well-chosen channels beats spreading thin over many.

Check what you just learned

1. What should drive channel choice?
  • What competitors do
  • The cheapest option
  • Where your persona spends time (correct)
  • Your favourite app

Go where your customers are.

Key terms: flip and sort

Funnel
The journey from awareness to loyalty
Owned media
Channels you control
Earned media
Exposure others give you
Paid media
Reach you buy
Conversion
A visitor taking the action you want
keyPoints: Choose channels from where the persona already is.
Do a few well, test small, then scale.

modules.title: Content and copywriting
modules.summary: Write clear, benefit-led copy with a strong headline and a call to action.
modules.outcome: You can write a headline, turn features into benefits, write a short advert and an email and end with a clear call to action.
modules.intro: People do not read websites and adverts; they scan. Good copy respects that: it opens with a promise, gets to the point and tells the reader what to do next.

topics.title: Headlines and benefits
topics.html:
The headline has one job: to earn the next sentence. The best headlines promise a benefit, are specific, and are short.

Features versus benefits
Feature (what it is)Benefit (what it does for you)
Free wifiFinish your assignment without using your data
Sockets at every tableNever leave your seat when your laptop runs low
Open until midnightStudy late without worrying about closing time
Worked example

Rewrite a headline

Weak: Chai and Co. Cafe. Better: Study fuel at student prices.

  1. The weak headline only names the cafe.
  2. The better one promises a benefit to a specific person.
  3. It is short and easy to remember.

Answer. Lead with what is in it for the reader, then give the name.

Headline checklist

  • Does it promise something the reader wants?
  • Is it specific, with a number where possible?
  • Could a competitor say the same thing? If yes, sharpen it.
  • Is it honest? Never promise what you cannot deliver.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is a benefit rather than a feature?
  • Free wifi
  • Open late
  • Sockets
  • Finish your assignment without using your data (correct)

A benefit says what it does for the reader.
keyPoints: A headline promises a specific benefit.
Translate features into benefits.

topics.title: Writing short copy
topics.html:
Rules of readable copy

  1. Use short sentences and everyday words.
  2. Write to one person: say you.
  3. One idea per paragraph.
  4. Put the most important point first.
  5. Cut every word that does not help.
  6. Read it aloud: if you stumble, so will the reader.
Worked example

Cut the copy

Before: We are very pleased to announce that we have now introduced a brand new student discount scheme at our cafe.

  1. Remove the filler: very pleased to announce.
  2. Say the point: students get 15% off.
  3. Result: Students get 15% off every cup.

Answer. Shorter is almost always stronger.

Try it yourself: Rewrite: In order to take advantage of this offer you will need to present a valid student identity card.

Model answer. Show your student ID to get the offer.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is the better line?
  • Students get 15% off (correct)
  • We are delighted to inform you of a discount
  • Offer inside
  • Please note a discount exists

It is short, specific and direct.
keyPoints: Short, direct, benefit-first writing; one idea per paragraph.
Cut filler words; read aloud.

topics.title: Calls to action
topics.html:
Definition

Call to action (CTA). The specific thing you want the reader to do next, written as a clear instruction, such as Order now or Show your ID.

Weak and strong CTAs
WeakStrong
Click hereGet my free study pack
SubmitBook my table
Learn moreSee the student menu
We hope to see youVisit us this week and bring a friend

A good CTA

  • Starts with a verb.
  • Says what the reader gets.
  • Is easy to find and to act on.
  • Creates a reason to act now, if there honestly is one (a real deadline).
Watch out

Do not invent fake urgency. 'Only 2 left' when there are hundreds, or a sale that never ends, is deceptive and damages trust.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is the strongest call to action?
  • Click here
  • Get my free study pack (correct)
  • Submit
  • More

It says what the reader gets.

Key terms: flip and sort

Headline
The line that earns the next sentence
Benefit
What something does for the customer
Feature
A fact about the product
Call to action
The next step you ask for
Copy
Writing meant to persuade or inform
keyPoints: A CTA starts with a verb and tells the reader what happens next.
Urgency must be true.

modules.title: Search, social and email
modules.summary: Learn what each of the three biggest digital channels does best, and the rules for using them fairly.
modules.outcome: You can explain how search, social media and email marketing work, write better subject lines and avoid common mistakes with permission and honesty.
modules.intro: Most digital marketing happens in three places: where people search, where they scroll and where they read their messages. Each rewards different habits.

topics.title: Search: be found by people who are looking
topics.html:
Search is unusual because the customer arrives with a need and is already looking. There are two ways to appear: organic results (earned by being relevant and trusted) and paid search adverts.

Organic and paid search
Organic (SEO)Paid search
CostTime and effort, no per-click feeYou pay each click
SpeedWeeks to monthsImmediate
LastsYes, while content stays goodOnly while you pay
Good forTrust, long-term trafficLaunches, offers, testing

Basics that help you be found

  • Use the words customers use in your titles and headings.
  • Answer real questions clearly.
  • Make pages fast and easy on a phone.
  • Keep your business name, address and phone the same everywhere.
  • Collect honest reviews.
Tip

Think of each search as a question. Your page must be the best answer to it.

Check what you just learned

1. Which is true of paid search?
  • It lasts forever
  • It is free
  • It stops when you stop paying (correct)
  • It cannot be targeted

You rent the traffic.
keyPoints: Search shows up when people are already looking.
Organic search builds over time; paid search is immediate.

topics.title: Social media marketing
topics.html:
Social media is a conversation, not a billboard. People go there to be entertained and to connect, so adverts that look like adverts are skipped.

Habits that work
HabitWhy
Show people, not just productsPeople connect with people
Post consistently, not constantlyA steady rhythm builds trust
Reply to comments and messagesIt is what makes it social
Use short video in the first seconds hookAttention is won quickly
Ask for and share customer content (with permission)It is earned, trusted media
Watch out

If a creator is paid or given free products to post about you, the post must be clearly marked as an advertisement. Hidden promotion is deceptive and, in many countries, against the rules.

Common mistakes

  • Posting only discounts.
  • Buying followers: fake followers do not buy.
  • Ignoring negative comments instead of answering them politely.

Check what you just learned

1. What must be done with a paid influencer post?
  • Hide that it is paid
  • Add more hashtags
  • Delete it
  • Clearly mark it as an advertisement (correct)

Disclosure is required.
keyPoints: Be social: show people, reply, post steadily.
Always disclose paid promotion.

topics.title: Email marketing and permission
topics.html:
Email gives a very high return because you reach people who chose to hear from you. Its two rules are permission and value.

The basics
RuleMeaning
PermissionOnly email people who agreed. Do not buy lists.
Clear senderSay who you are in the From name.
Honest subjectDo not mislead to get opens.
Easy unsubscribeA visible link in every email; honour it at once.
ValueEach email should be useful or interesting.

Writing subject lines

  • Be specific: what is inside?
  • Keep to about 40 characters so phones show it all.
  • Avoid ALL CAPITALS and many exclamation marks.
  • Never fake a reply (Re:) or urgency.
  • Test two versions on a small part of the list.
Watch out

Privacy laws in many countries require consent and an unsubscribe option. Check the rules where your customers live.

Check what you just learned

1. Before emailing a customer you need their:
  • Permission (correct)
  • Address only
  • Birthday
  • Photo

Consent is the foundation.

Key terms: flip and sort

Organic
Results earned without paying for each click
Paid search
Adverts shown for searches, paid per click
Opt-in
A person agreeing to receive messages
Unsubscribe
A person opting out
Subject line
The title of an email
keyPoints: Email needs permission, honesty and an easy unsubscribe.
Good subject lines are specific and short.

modules.title: Measure and optimise
modules.summary: Track the numbers that matter, run a fair test and decide where to put your next rupee.
modules.outcome: You can calculate CTR, CPC, conversion rate, CPA and ROAS, run and read an A/B test and allocate a budget.
modules.intro: Digital marketing is measurable, which is its great strength. But there are many numbers, and most do not matter. This module teaches the few that guide decisions.

topics.title: The numbers that matter
topics.html:
Core metrics
MetricFormulaTells you
Click-through rate (CTR)clicks / impressionsHow appealing the advert is
Cost per click (CPC)spend / clicksWhat each visit costs
Conversion ratesales / clicksHow well the page turns visitors into customers
Cost per acquisition (CPA)spend / salesWhat each sale costs
Return on ad spend (ROAS)revenue / spendRupees back for each rupee spent

Change the inputs, see the ratios

Try different spend, clicks and sales and watch cost per sale and ROAS.

Adjust Spend (rupees), Clicks, Sales, Average sale (rupees) and see Cost per click, Conversion rate, Cost per sale, ROAS change.

Watch out

Vanity metrics such as likes and follower counts feel good but do not pay bills. Prefer numbers tied to sales.

Check what you just learned

1. ROAS of 3 means:
  • 3 clicks per sale
  • 3 rupees of revenue per rupee spent (correct)
  • A 3% rate
  • 3 sales

Revenue divided by spend.

2. Cost per acquisition is:
  • Spend per click
  • Revenue per click
  • Spend per sale (correct)
  • Clicks per view

What each customer cost.
keyPoints: CTR, CPC, conversion rate, CPA and ROAS guide decisions.
Prefer metrics tied to sales over vanity metrics.

topics.title: A/B testing
topics.html:
An A/B test shows two versions to similar visitors at the same time and compares their results. Change one thing at a time (a headline, a button) so you know what caused the difference.

An example
VersionVisitorsOrdersRate
A (current)2,400964.0%
B (new button)2,5001255.0%
Formula · Lift

lift = (rate B - rate A) / rate A

Here (5.0 - 4.0) / 4.0 = 25% better.

Cautions

  • With few visitors, differences can be luck, so do not stop early.
  • Run for at least a full week to cover weekday and weekend behaviour.
  • A win in clicks may not be a win in sales: test what matters.
  • Write down what you learned, even from tests that fail.

Check what you just learned

1. Why change only one thing in a test?
  • It is faster
  • It is required by law
  • It is cheaper
  • So you know what caused the difference (correct)

Otherwise causes are mixed.
keyPoints: Test one change at a time on similar visitors at the same time.
Small tests can mislead; run long enough.

topics.title: Budgets and decisions
topics.html:
Measuring is only useful if it changes what you do. A simple rule: move money towards what works and away from what does not, while keeping a small share for testing new things.

A starting split for 1,00,000 a month
UseShareAmount
Proven channels60%60,000
Promising channels25%25,000
Tests and new ideas15%15,000
Worked example

Reallocate

Search ads return 3 rupees per rupee spent; social ads return 2; email returns 37.

  1. Email is far more efficient, but it is limited by the size of your list.
  2. Move some budget to growing the list.
  3. Keep search running while it is profitable.
  4. Cut or fix the weakest channel after a fair test.

Answer. Efficiency tells you where to invest next, and the list size tells you where it will run out.

Common mistakes

  • Judging a channel after two days.
  • Cutting a channel that feeds the others (such as awareness) because it does not show direct sales.
  • Never testing anything new.
Tip

Review the numbers on the same day every week and write one decision after each review.

Check what you just learned

1. A sensible share of budget to reserve for new tests is about:
  • 10 to 15% (correct)
  • 0%
  • 90%
  • 100%

A small share keeps you learning.

Key terms: flip and sort

CTR
Click-through rate
CPC
Cost per click
Conversion rate
Share of visitors who take the action
CPA
Cost per acquisition
ROAS
Return on ad spend
A/B test
A fair comparison of two versions
keyPoints: Move money towards what works; keep a share for testing.
Do not judge too early or ignore a channel's role in the funnel.

modules.title: Plan a campaign
modules.summary: Turn everything into one page: a goal, an audience, a message, channels, a budget and a way of measuring it, within honest rules.
modules.outcome: You can write a campaign brief, set a goal that can be measured and run it honestly and legally.
modules.intro: A campaign is a plan with a start, an end and a purpose. The brief is the document that keeps everyone pointing the same way.

topics.title: Setting a goal that can be measured
topics.html:
SMART goals
LetterMeaningExample
SpecificSays exactly whatBring students into the cafe
MeasurableHas a number300 student discounts redeemed
AchievablePossible with your resourcesAbout 20 a day
RelevantMatters to the businessFills quiet afternoon hours
Time-boundHas a deadlineBetween 1 and 14 August
Worked example

From vague to SMART

Vague: get more customers. SMART: bring 300 student visits to the cafe between 1 and 14 August, measured by ID discounts used.

  1. It names the group (students).
  2. It has a number (300) and dates.
  3. It says how it will be counted.

Answer. A SMART goal tells you on the last day whether you succeeded.

Tip

Write the goal before the creative ideas. A goal makes it easy to reject ideas that do not serve it.

Check what you just learned

1. Which goal is SMART?
  • Be popular
  • Get 300 student visits by 14 August (correct)
  • Sell more
  • Do well

It has a number, a group and a deadline.
keyPoints: SMART goals are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
Set the goal before choosing the ideas.

topics.title: The campaign brief
topics.html:
Six sections of a one-page brief

  1. Goal: the measurable result and the dates.
  2. Audience: who it is for (your persona).
  3. Message: the single thing to say and the offer.
  4. Channels: where and how people will see it.
  5. Budget: the total and how it is split.
  6. Measures: the numbers you will check and when.

A good brief fits on one page. If it takes ten, nobody will read it. Include a calendar showing what happens each day, who is responsible and when you will review.

Common mistakes

  • Starting to design before the goal is agreed.
  • Having several messages in one campaign.
  • Not saying how success will be measured.

Check what you just learned

1. How many main messages should a campaign have?
  • As many as possible
  • Five
  • One (correct)
  • None

A single message is remembered.
keyPoints: A brief covers goal, audience, message, channels, budget and measures.
One page; one message.

topics.title: Honesty, privacy and the rules
topics.html:
Marketing works because customers trust it. Break that trust and the damage lasts longer than any campaign. Most countries have rules, and the principles are similar everywhere.

Principles
PrincipleIn practice
TruthfulDo not make claims you cannot support
Clear termsState conditions of an offer plainly (dates, limits, who qualifies)
DisclosedMark paid endorsements and sponsored content
Consent and privacyCollect data only with permission; explain how you use it; keep it safe
RespectAvoid stereotypes and targeting vulnerable people unfairly

Quick checks before launch

  1. Can I prove every claim?
  2. Are the terms of the offer visible?
  3. Is every paid post labelled?
  4. Do I have permission to contact these people?
  5. Would I be comfortable explaining this to the customer's face?
Watch out

Laws differ by country and change. Check the rules of the places where your customers live, or ask a qualified adviser, before you launch.

Check what you just learned

1. A paid influencer post should be:
  • Hidden
  • Edited later
  • Removed
  • Labelled as an advertisement (correct)

Disclosure protects trust and complies with the rules.

Key terms: flip and sort

SMART goal
Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound
Campaign brief
A one-page plan
Disclosure
Saying a post is paid
Consent
Permission to contact or use data
keyPoints: Be truthful, disclose paid content, get consent and keep terms clear.
Rules differ by country: check them.
